category.name: Engineering
category.tagline: From KVL to Bernoulli to K-maps: core formulas, real numbers and classic exam traps

packs.title: Circuit Analysis
packs.description: Dividers, node vs mesh, Thévenin/Norton, max power, superposition, op-amp gains, C and L behavior, first-order transients, impedance, RMS.

cards.title: A 10 Ω resistor carries 2 A. How much power does it absorb?
cards.body:
40 W.
V = IR = 20 V, so P = VI = 40 W. Same from P = I²R = 4·10 or P = V²/R = 400/10.
Pick whichever form uses the quantities you know. With the passive sign convention a resistor's p = i²R is never negative: it only absorbs.

cards.title: Passive sign convention: current enters an element's + terminal and p = vi = −12 W. Is the element absorbing or delivering power?
cards.body:
Delivering (supplying) 12 W.
When current enters the + terminal, p = vi is the power absorbed: p > 0 absorbs, p < 0 delivers. Absorbing −12 W is the same as delivering +12 W.
If current enters the − terminal, use p = −vi. Alexander/Sadiku and Nilsson/Riedel both use this convention.

cards.title: 12 V is applied across 4 kΩ and 2 kΩ resistors in series. What is the voltage across the 2 kΩ resistor?
cards.body:
4 V.
Voltage divider: v₂ = V_s·R₂/(R₁ + R₂) = 12·2/6 = 4 V; the 4 kΩ resistor takes the other 8 V. The larger resistor gets the larger share.
Only valid if nothing draws current from the midpoint: a load across R₂ must first be combined in parallel with R₂.

cards.title: 9 A splits between 3 Ω and 6 Ω resistors in parallel. How much current flows through the 3 Ω resistor?
cards.body:
6 A.
Current divider: i₁ = I·R₂/(R₁ + R₂) = 9·6/9 = 6 A. The numerator is the OTHER resistor, so the smaller resistance carries more current.
Check: R_eq = R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂) = 2 Ω, v = 9·2 = 18 V, and 18/3 = 6 A.

cards.title: Node-voltage vs mesh-current analysis: which Kirchhoff law does each method apply, and what are the unknowns?
cards.body:
Node-voltage: KCL at each non-reference node; unknowns are node voltages (N − 1 of them). Works for any circuit.
Mesh-current: KVL around each mesh; unknowns are mesh currents (B − N + 1 of them). Planar circuits only.
Voltage source between two non-reference nodes → supernode; current source shared by two meshes → supermesh.

cards.title: Superposition lets you add the voltages and currents produced by each independent source acting alone. What can you NOT add this way?
cards.body:
Power.
p = i²R is nonlinear: (i₁ + i₂)²R ≠ i₁²R + i₂²R. Superpose the currents or voltages first, then compute power.
Superposition needs a linear circuit: turn off the other independent sources (V → short, I → open) but leave dependent sources on. (Exception: average powers from sources of different frequencies do add.)

cards.title: Finding R_th by turning sources off: what replaces an independent voltage source, an independent current source, and a dependent source?
cards.body:
Voltage source → short circuit (v = 0). Current source → open circuit (i = 0). Dependent sources are never turned off.
With dependent sources present, use R_th = v_oc/i_sc, or turn off only the independent sources, apply a test source and take R_th = v_test/i_test.
Norton equivalent: R_N = R_th, I_N = i_sc = V_th/R_th.

cards.title: A source has V_th = 20 V and R_th = 5 Ω. What is the maximum power it can deliver to a load resistor?
cards.body:
20 W, when R_L = R_th = 5 Ω.
P_max = V_th²/(4R_th) = 400/20 = 20 W (check: i = 20/10 = 2 A, P = 2²·5 = 20 W).
Trap: V_th²/R_th = 80 W. At maximum power transfer the efficiency is only 50%: R_th dissipates as much as the load.

cards.title: What two rules let you analyze an ideal op-amp circuit that has negative feedback?
cards.body:
1) No current flows into either input: i₊ = i₋ = 0 (infinite input resistance).
2) The two input voltages are equal: v₊ = v₋ (virtual short), from the infinite open-loop gain plus negative feedback.
Write KCL at the input nodes, not at the output node: the op-amp's output current is an extra unknown (it supplies whatever is needed), and v_o must stay within the supply rails.

cards.title: An inverting op-amp amplifier has R_in = 2 kΩ and R_f = 10 kΩ. What is its voltage gain v_o/v_in?
cards.body:
−5.
v_o/v_in = −R_f/R_in = −10/2. Derivation: v₋ = v₊ = 0 (virtual ground), so KCL at the − input gives v_in/R_in = −v_o/R_f.
The minus sign means the output is inverted. The input resistance seen by the source is just R_in.

cards.title: A non-inverting op-amp amplifier has R_f = 4 kΩ (output to − input) and R₁ = 1 kΩ (− input to ground). What is its gain?
cards.body:
5.
v_o/v_in = 1 + R_f/R₁ = 1 + 4 = 5. The output drives a divider: v₋ = v_o·R₁/(R₁ + R_f), and v₋ = v₊ = v_in.
Trap: answering R_f/R₁ = 4. The gain is always ≥ 1; with R_f = 0 (or R₁ removed) it's a voltage follower with gain 1.

cards.title: At DC steady state, an ideal capacitor behaves like what circuit element?
cards.body:
An open circuit.
i = C dv/dt, and at DC steady state v is constant, so i = 0. It still holds its charge and stored energy w = ½Cv².
Dual: an inductor (v = L di/dt) acts as a short circuit at DC steady state and stores w = ½Li².

cards.title: At a switching instant, which cannot change instantaneously in an inductor: its voltage or its current?
cards.body:
Its current: i_L(0⁺) = i_L(0⁻).
v = L di/dt, so a jump in current would need an infinite voltage. The inductor's voltage, by contrast, can jump.
Dual: a capacitor's voltage is continuous, v_C(0⁺) = v_C(0⁻), while its current can jump.

cards.title: In a first-order RC or RL circuit switched at t = 0, what is the general form of any response x(t) for t > 0?
cards.body:
x(t) = x(∞) + [x(0⁺) − x(∞)]e^(−t/τ)
τ = R_th·C for RC, or L/R_th for RL, where R_th is the Thévenin resistance seen by the C or L.
After 1τ about 63.2% of the change is done; after 5τ, more than 99%. Get x(0⁺) from the continuity of v_C or i_L.

cards.title: What is the impedance of a 1 μF capacitor at ω = 1000 rad/s?
cards.body:
−j1000 Ω (−j1 kΩ).
Z_C = 1/(jωC) = −j/(ωC) = −j/(1000·10⁻⁶). Inductor: Z_L = jωL.
Limits: as ω → 0, |Z_C| → ∞ (open at DC) and Z_L → 0 (short). The −j means the capacitor's current leads its voltage by 90°.

cards.title: What is the RMS value of v(t) = 170 cos(377t) V?
cards.body:
≈ 120 V.
For a pure sinusoid, V_rms = V_m/√2 ≈ 0.707·V_m = 170/1.414 ≈ 120.2 V. (377 rad/s = 60 Hz: US household voltage.)
This applies only to a sinusoid with no DC offset. Average power to a resistor: P = V_rms²/R.

packs.title: Statics
packs.description: Varignon, couples, moments about an axis, FBDs and supports, trusses, distributed loads, determinacy, friction (incline, tipping, belts), centroids.

cards.title: A force with components F_x = 3 kN and F_y = 4 kN acts at point (2 m, 1 m). Its moment about the origin, counterclockwise positive?
cards.body:
+5 kN·m (counterclockwise).
Varignon's theorem: add the moments of the components. F_y has arm x = 2 m (CCW, +8); F_x has arm y = 1 m (CW, −3). M_O = xF_y − yF_x = 8 − 3 = 5 kN·m, the z-component of r × F.
Trap: adding both (11 kN·m). Check with M = F·d: F = 5 kN and its line of action passes d = 1 m from O.

cards.title: Equal and opposite forces F act along parallel lines a perpendicular distance d apart. What is their moment about any point P?
cards.body:
M = Fd, the same about every point.
The pair (a couple) has zero resultant force, and its moment doesn't depend on the reference point, so a couple moment is a free vector: it can be applied anywhere on a rigid body with the same external effect.
Two couples are equivalent if their moments have the same magnitude and direction.

cards.title: A distributed load increases linearly from 0 at A to 6 kN/m at B, 3 m away. How far from A does its resultant act?
cards.body:
2 m from A (1 m from B).
Resultant = area under the load curve = ½(6 kN/m)(3 m) = 9 kN, acting through the centroid of that area. A triangle's centroid is 1/3 of the length from its tall end, i.e., 2/3 from the zero end.
Uniform load w over length L: resultant wL at the midpoint.

cards.title: On a free-body diagram, which forces must you show, and which must you leave off?
cards.body:
Show every external force and couple on the isolated body: applied loads, the weight at the center of gravity, and the reactions at every support or connection you cut away.
Leave off internal forces (they cancel in pairs) and forces the body exerts on other bodies.
Assume a sense for each unknown; a negative answer just means it acts the other way.

cards.title: In 2D, how many reaction components does each support provide: a roller, a smooth pin, and a fixed support?
cards.body:
Roller: 1 (a force normal to the surface). Pin: 2 (force components A_x and A_y; it lets the member rotate, so no moment). Fixed: 3 (A_x, A_y and a couple moment M_A).
Rule: a support exerts a force for each direction of translation it prevents and a couple moment for each rotation it prevents.

cards.title: How many independent equilibrium equations can you write for one rigid body in a 2D (coplanar) problem?
cards.body:
3: ΣF_x = 0, ΣF_y = 0, ΣM_O = 0, so one 2D free-body diagram can solve at most 3 unknowns. In 3D there are 6 (three force sums, three moment sums).
Alternative 2D sets: ΣF_x, ΣM_A, ΣM_B (line AB not perpendicular to x) or ΣM_A, ΣM_B, ΣM_C (A, B, C not collinear).

cards.title: A pin-connected member has no loads between its two ends and negligible weight. What must be true of the forces at its ends?
cards.body:
They are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, and collinear along the line joining the two pins, so the member is in pure tension or compression.
Why: summing moments about one pin forces the other pin's force to pass through it.
For a curved or bent two-force member, the force still acts along the straight line between the pins, not along the member.

cards.title: A 2D beam is supported by a pin at A and rollers at B and C. What is its degree of static indeterminacy?
cards.body:
1 (indeterminate to the first degree).
Unknown reactions: 2 + 1 + 1 = 4, but equilibrium gives only 3 equations, so degree = 4 − 3 = 1. The extra equation comes from deformation (compatibility), as in Mechanics of Materials.
Exactly 3 reactions isn't enough on its own: if they are all parallel or all concurrent, the body is improperly constrained.

cards.title: Truss analysis: when is the method of sections faster than the method of joints?
cards.body:
When you need only a few member forces deep inside the truss.
Sections: cut through no more than 3 members with unknown forces and apply all 3 equilibrium equations to one side; take moments about the point where two unknown forces intersect.
Joints: 2 equations (ΣF_x, ΣF_y) per pin, so start at a joint with at most 2 unknowns. Assume tension; a negative result means compression.

cards.title: A truss joint with no external load or support connects three members, two of them collinear. What is the force in the third member?
cards.body:
Zero.
Sum forces perpendicular to the collinear pair: only the third member has a component in that direction, so its force must be 0.
Other rule: an unloaded, unsupported joint with only two non-collinear members makes both zero-force members. They still matter: they brace the truss and carry load if the loading changes.

cards.title: A block on an incline is on the verge of sliding when the incline angle reaches θ. What is the coefficient of static friction?
cards.body:
μ_s = tan θ.
Along the slope: W sin θ = μ_s N; normal to it: N = W cos θ. Dividing gives μ_s = tan θ, independent of the weight.
This θ is the angle of repose, equal to the friction angle φ_s = tan⁻¹ μ_s.

cards.title: A uniform crate is pushed horizontally. How do you decide whether it slides or tips first?
cards.body:
Find the push P for each case separately; the smaller P happens first.
Sliding: static friction (F ≤ μ_s N) reaches its maximum, so P = μ_s W (level floor).
Tipping: the normal force and friction shift to the leading bottom corner; moments about that corner give P·h = W·b/2 (base width b, push at height h).
If a computed normal-force location falls outside the base, tipping governs.

cards.title: A rope wrapped around a fixed drum is on the verge of slipping. How is the tight-side tension T₂ related to the slack-side tension T₁?
cards.body:
T₂ = T₁·e^(μ_s·β), where β is the contact angle in RADIANS (each full wrap adds 2π) and T₂ is on the side toward which slipping impends.
Tension grows exponentially with wrap: with μ_s = 0.3, two full wraps (β = 4π) give T₂/T₁ = e^3.77 ≈ 43, which is how a capstan lets one person hold a heavy load.
It doesn't depend on the drum's radius.

cards.title: How do you find the centroid of a composite area that has a hole cut out of it?
cards.body:
x̄ = Σx̃A/ΣA (same for ȳ), where x̃ is the centroid of each simple part.
Treat the hole as a negative area: subtract both its A and its x̃A.
Handy parts: rectangle at its middle, triangle at h/3 from its base, semicircle at 4r/(3π) from its diameter. The centroid lies on any axis of symmetry.

cards.title: How do you find the moment of a force F about a specified axis a, rather than about a point?
cards.body:
M_a = u_a·(r × F), a scalar triple product: u_a is the unit vector along the axis, and r runs from ANY point on the axis to ANY point on F's line of action.
Only the part of F perpendicular to the axis that doesn't intersect it causes rotation about it: a force parallel to the axis, or one crossing it, has zero moment about that axis.

packs.title: Mechanics of Materials
packs.description: E and ν values, axial and thermal loading, torsion, bending and shear stress, beam deflection, Mohr's circle and Euler buckling, with worked numbers.

cards.title: Hooke's law σ = Eε: what is the approximate modulus of elasticity of structural steel, and of aluminum alloys?
cards.body:
Steel ≈ 200 GPa (29,000 ksi); aluminum ≈ 70 GPa (10,000 ksi), about 1/3 of steel.
So at the same stress, aluminum strains about 3× as much. E is the slope of the linear-elastic part of the σ–ε curve: it measures stiffness, not strength.
σ = Eε holds only up to the proportional limit.

cards.title: Tension test of mild steel: name the four regions of the engineering stress–strain curve, in order.
cards.body:
Elastic → yielding → strain hardening → necking.
Key points: proportional limit and yield stress σ_Y (end of elastic behavior), ultimate stress σ_u (the peak), then fracture.
Engineering stress drops during necking only because it divides by the original area; the true stress keeps rising until fracture.

cards.title: A bar stretched axially to a longitudinal strain of 0.001 has Poisson's ratio ν = 0.3. What is its lateral strain?
cards.body:
−0.0003 (−300 × 10⁻⁶): it gets thinner as it stretches.
ν = −ε_lat/ε_long, so ε_lat = −ν·ε_long. The minus sign is the usual trap.
Hibbeler: 0 ≤ ν ≤ 0.5. Metals are about 0.25–0.35 (steel ≈ 0.3); ν = 0.5 means incompressible (rubber-like).

cards.title: A steel rod (E = 200 GPa) with A = 100 mm² and L = 2 m carries an axial load of 10 kN. How much does it elongate?
cards.body:
1 mm.
δ = PL/(AE) = (10,000 N)(2000 mm)/[(100 mm²)(200,000 N/mm²)] = 1 mm. N and mm are convenient because 1 MPa = 1 N/mm², so 200 GPa = 200,000 N/mm².
Valid in the linear-elastic range with constant P, A and E; otherwise sum PL/(AE) over segments.

cards.title: A steel bar (E = 200 GPa, α = 12 × 10⁻⁶/°C) is held between rigid walls and heated 50 °C. Magnitude of the thermal stress?
cards.body:
120 MPa, compressive.
The free thermal strain αΔT = 600 × 10⁻⁶ is completely prevented, so σ = EαΔT = (200,000 MPa)(600 × 10⁻⁶) = 120 MPa.
The bar's length and area don't matter. If the bar were free to expand, the stress would be zero: thermal strain alone causes no stress.

cards.title: Hooke's law in shear is τ = Gγ. How is G related to E and Poisson's ratio ν for an isotropic material?
cards.body:
G = E/[2(1 + ν)].
Steel: 200/(2·1.3) ≈ 77 GPa (Hibbeler's A-36 table value: 75 GPa). Since 0 ≤ ν ≤ 0.5, G always lies between E/3 and E/2.
γ is the shear strain in radians: the change in an originally right angle.

cards.title: What is the polar moment of inertia J of a solid circular shaft of diameter d?
cards.body:
J = πd⁴/32 = πc⁴/2 (c = radius).
It sets the torsion stress τ = Tρ/J, which grows linearly from 0 at the center to τ_max = Tc/J at the surface.
Hollow shaft: J = (π/2)(c_o⁴ − c_i⁴). Trap: πd⁴/64 is I about a diameter; J = 2I.

cards.title: Angle of twist φ of a uniform circular shaft of length L under torque T (shear modulus G)?
cards.body:
φ = TL/(GJ), in radians.
Same pattern as axial δ = PL/(AE). For several segments, sum TᵢLᵢ/(GᵢJᵢ) using each segment's internal torque, positive by the right-hand rule when the thumb points out of the cut section.
Valid for linear-elastic circular shafts.

cards.title: Twisted to failure, how does the fracture surface of a ductile shaft differ from that of a brittle one?
cards.body:
Ductile (mild steel): a flat break perpendicular to the axis. It fails in shear, which is maximum on transverse planes.
Brittle (cast iron, chalk): a 45° helix. It fails in tension, because pure shear produces σ₁ = τ on planes at 45°.
Ductile = large plastic strain before fracture; brittle = little or no yielding, and much stronger in compression than in tension.

cards.title: Beam relations: how is the bending moment M related to the shear V, and V to the distributed load w?
cards.body:
dM/dx = V and dV/dx = −w, with w the downward load intensity (Hibbeler takes w positive upward and writes dV/dx = w).
So M has a local max or min where V = 0, the change in M between two points = area under the V diagram, and ΔV = −(area under the downward load).
A point force makes V jump; a concentrated couple makes M jump.

cards.title: Area moment of inertia of a b × h rectangle about its centroidal axis parallel to side b?
cards.body:
I = bh³/12, where h is the dimension perpendicular to the bending axis.
A 50 × 200 mm board is 16× stiffer on edge than laid flat: (200/50)² = 16.
Other parallel axes: I = Ī + Ad², with Ī about the centroid (e.g., bh³/3 about the base).

cards.title: Flexure formula: what is the bending stress at distance y above the neutral axis, and which side is compressed by a positive moment?
cards.body:
σ = −My/I (Hibbeler: y measured upward, positive M = sagging, concave up). A positive moment compresses the top and stretches the bottom.
Stress varies linearly: zero at the neutral axis (through the centroid), maximum σ = Mc/I at the extreme fiber.
Assumes linear-elastic, homogeneous material and a section symmetric about the plane of loading.

cards.title: From τ = VQ/(It), what is the maximum transverse shear stress in a rectangular section of area A carrying shear V?
cards.body:
τ_max = 1.5V/A, at the neutral axis; the distribution is parabolic, zero at the top and bottom.
Q = ȳ′A′, the first moment about the neutral axis of the area beyond the point; t = section width there. At the NA, Q = bh²/8, so τ = V(bh²/8)/[(bh³/12)b] = 1.5V/(bh).
Trap: V/A is only the average.

cards.title: Maximum deflection of a cantilever (length L, flexural rigidity EI) carrying a point load P at its free end?
cards.body:
δ_max = PL³/(3EI), at the free end (slope there: PL²/(2EI)).
Deflection ∝ L³: doubling the length gives 8× the deflection.
Compare a simply supported beam with P at midspan: PL³/(48EI). Mnemonic: each half acts like a cantilever of length L/2 carrying P/2.

cards.title: Plane stress: σ_x = 100 MPa, σ_y = 20 MPa, τ_xy = 30 MPa. What is the maximum in-plane shear stress?
cards.body:
50 MPa, the radius of Mohr's circle.
Center σ_avg = (σ_x + σ_y)/2 = 60 MPa; R = √[((σ_x − σ_y)/2)² + τ_xy²] = √(40² + 30²) = 50 MPa. Principal stresses: 60 ± 50 = 110 and 10 MPa.
Both are tensile, so the absolute maximum shear (out of plane, with σ₃ = 0) is 110/2 = 55 MPa.

cards.title: Euler critical load of a long, slender column of length L with both ends pinned?
cards.body:
P_cr = π²EI/L², with I the SMALLEST moment of inertia (it buckles about the weak axis).
Other end conditions: P_cr = π²EI/(KL)² with K = 2 (fixed–free), 0.7 (fixed–pinned), 0.5 (fixed–fixed).
Valid only if σ_cr = P_cr/A stays below the proportional limit (elastic buckling).

packs.title: Engineering Thermodynamics
packs.description: Systems, first-law signs, quality, ideal-gas relations, boundary work, nozzles and throttling, second law, Carnot, COP, entropy, Otto and Rankine.

cards.title: What type of thermodynamic system allows neither mass nor energy to cross its boundary?
cards.body:
An isolated system.
Closed system (control mass): energy can cross as heat or work, but mass cannot, e.g., gas in a piston–cylinder.
Open system (control volume): both mass and energy cross, e.g., turbines, nozzles, pumps.

cards.title: Are heat and work state (point) functions or path functions, and what does that mean?
cards.body:
Path functions: their amounts depend on the process path, not just the end states. Write δQ and δW, and Q₁₂ or W₁₂, never ΔQ or ΔW.
Properties (P, T, v, u, h, s) are state functions: ΔU depends only on the end states, so ∮dU = 0 over a cycle, while the net work of a cycle generally isn't zero.

cards.title: A closed system receives 50 kJ of heat and does 20 kJ of work on its surroundings. What is ΔU (no KE or PE change)?
cards.body:
+30 kJ.
Sign convention used (Çengel): Q − W = ΔU + ΔKE + ΔPE, with Q = net heat transfer TO the system and W = net work done BY the system: 50 − 20 = 30 kJ.
Many chemistry texts write ΔU = Q + W with W done ON the system: same physics, opposite sign on W.

cards.title: What is the quality x of a saturated liquid–vapor mixture, and how do you find it from the specific volume v?
cards.body:
x = m_vapor/m_total (0 = saturated liquid, 1 = saturated vapor); it's defined only under the vapor dome.
v = v_f + x·v_fg, so x = (v − v_f)/(v_g − v_f). Same pattern for u, h and s.
Example, water at 100 °C: v_f = 0.001043, v_g = 1.6720 m³/kg; v = 0.5 m³/kg gives x ≈ 0.30.

cards.title: For an ideal gas, what does c_p − c_v equal?
cards.body:
R, the specific gas constant (R = R_u/M, with R_u = 8.314 kJ/kmol·K).
Air: R = 0.287, c_p ≈ 1.005 and c_v ≈ 0.718 kJ/kg·K at room temperature, so k = c_p/c_v ≈ 1.4.
Ideal-gas u and h depend on T only: Δu = c_v ΔT and Δh = c_p ΔT for ANY process (constant specific heats), not just constant-volume or constant-pressure ones.

cards.title: Boundary work done by an ideal gas expanding isothermally in a closed system from V₁ to V₂?
cards.body:
W_b = mRT ln(V₂/V₁) = P₁V₁ ln(V₂/V₁) = mRT ln(P₁/P₂).
It's ∫P dV with P = mRT/V. In general W_b = area under the process curve on a P–V diagram (constant P: P(V₂ − V₁); 1 kPa·m³ = 1 kJ).
Isothermal ideal gas: ΔU = 0, so Q = W_b.

cards.title: Why do control-volume (open-system) energy balances use enthalpy h instead of internal energy u?
cards.body:
h = u + Pv, and Pv is the flow work (flow energy) needed to push each kilogram of fluid across the boundary.
So each unit mass of flowing fluid carries energy h + V²/2 + gz.
Ideal gas: Δh = c_p ΔT. For a closed system at constant pressure with only boundary work, Q = ΔH.

cards.title: Air enters an adiabatic nozzle at negligible velocity, and its enthalpy drops by 20 kJ/kg. What is the exit velocity?
cards.body:
200 m/s.
Steady flow, no work or heat, ΔPE ≈ 0: V₂²/2 = h₁ − h₂ = 20 kJ/kg = 20,000 m²/s², so V₂ = √40,000 = 200 m/s.
Trap: forgetting 1 kJ/kg = 1000 m²/s² gives √40 ≈ 6.3 m/s. A diffuser does the reverse: it slows the flow and raises h and P.

cards.title: Across an adiabatic throttling valve (no work, negligible KE and PE change), which property stays constant?
cards.body:
Enthalpy: h₁ = h₂ (isenthalpic).
For an ideal gas h = h(T), so T stays constant too. A real fluid such as a refrigerant drops sharply in pressure and temperature, partly flashing to vapor: that's the expansion valve in a refrigerator.
Entropy increases: throttling is highly irreversible.

cards.title: State the Kelvin–Planck and the Clausius statements of the second law.
cards.body:
Kelvin–Planck: no device operating in a cycle can receive heat from a single reservoir and produce a net amount of work, so no heat engine has η_th = 100%.
Clausius: no cyclic device can have, as its sole effect, heat transfer from a colder body to a hotter one, so a refrigerator needs a work input.
The two are equivalent: violating one violates the other.

cards.title: Maximum possible thermal efficiency of a heat engine operating between reservoirs at 527 °C and 27 °C?
cards.body:
62.5%.
η_Carnot = 1 − T_L/T_H with ABSOLUTE temperatures: 1 − 300 K/800 K = 0.625.
Trap: plugging in °C gives 1 − 27/527 ≈ 95%. Every real (irreversible) engine between the same two reservoirs does worse.

cards.title: A refrigeration cycle has COP_R = 3. What is its COP when the same cycle (same Q_L, Q_H, W) is used as a heat pump?
cards.body:
4.
COP_R = Q_L/W_in and COP_HP = Q_H/W_in = (Q_L + W_in)/W_in = COP_R + 1.
COPs above 1 are normal; COP isn't an efficiency. Reversible (Carnot) limits, with absolute temperatures: COP_R = T_L/(T_H − T_L) and COP_HP = T_H/(T_H − T_L).

cards.title: An analysis of a proposed process gives entropy generation S_gen < 0. What can you conclude?
cards.body:
The process is impossible: it violates the second law.
S_gen > 0: irreversible (every real process); S_gen = 0: reversible (an idealization); S_gen < 0: impossible.
Trap: a system's own entropy CAN decrease when heat leaves it. Only S_gen, equivalently ΔS of an isolated system, can never be negative.

cards.title: For an ideal gas with constant specific heats undergoing an isentropic process, what combination of P and V stays constant?
cards.body:
PVᵏ (equivalently Pvᵏ), with k = c_p/c_v ≈ 1.4 for air.
Also T₂/T₁ = (P₂/P₁)^((k−1)/k) = (v₁/v₂)^(k−1).
Isentropic = reversible AND adiabatic. Trap: PV = constant is the isothermal ideal-gas process, not the isentropic one.

cards.title: Cold-air-standard Otto cycle: thermal efficiency in terms of compression ratio r and specific heat ratio k?
cards.body:
η = 1 − 1/r^(k−1).
r = V_max/V_min. Example: r = 8, k = 1.4 gives 1 − 8^(−0.4) ≈ 0.565 (56.5%).
Efficiency rises with r, but real spark-ignition engines can't raise r much because of engine knock (autoignition of the fuel–air mixture).

cards.title: List the four components of the ideal Rankine cycle in flow order, with the ideal process in each.
cards.body:
Pump (isentropic compression of liquid) → boiler (constant-pressure heat addition) → turbine (isentropic expansion) → condenser (constant-pressure heat rejection).
Pump work is tiny next to turbine work because liquid v is small: w_pump ≈ v(P₂ − P₁).
η_th = w_net/q_in = 1 − q_out/q_in.

packs.title: Fluid Mechanics
packs.description: Viscosity, hydrostatics, buoyancy, center of pressure, continuity, Bernoulli and Pitot tubes, Reynolds number, friction factor, head loss, drag scaling.

cards.title: A liquid has density 850 kg/m³. What is its specific gravity?
cards.body:
0.85.
SG = ρ/ρ_water, with ρ_water = 1000 kg/m³ (at 4 °C); it's dimensionless.
Specific weight is different: γ = ρg, in N/m³. Water: γ ≈ 9.81 kN/m³; this liquid: 850·9.81 ≈ 8.34 kN/m³.

cards.title: What does the no-slip condition say about a viscous fluid in contact with a solid surface?
cards.body:
The fluid sticks to the surface: its velocity relative to the surface is zero (at a stationary wall, u = 0).
This creates the steep velocity gradient near walls (the boundary layer), hence wall shear stress τ_w = μ(du/dy) at the wall, friction drag and pipe head loss.
Inviscid (Bernoulli) analyses can't satisfy it.

cards.title: Oil (μ = 0.1 Pa·s) fills a 2 mm gap between a fixed wall and a plate moving at 0.4 m/s. Shear stress on the plate (linear profile)?
cards.body:
20 Pa.
Newton's law of viscosity: τ = μ du/dy. No-slip makes the velocity go from 0 to 0.4 m/s across the gap: du/dy = 0.4/0.002 = 200 s⁻¹, so τ = 0.1·200 = 20 Pa.
Units: 1 Pa·s = 1 N·s/m² = 1 kg/(m·s). Newtonian fluids (water, air, oils) have τ linear in du/dy.

cards.title: Kinematic viscosity ν equals the dynamic viscosity μ divided by what?
cards.body:
Density: ν = μ/ρ, in m²/s (1 stoke = 1 cm²/s).
At 20 °C: water ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s, air ≈ 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s. Air's ν is ~15× water's even though its μ is ~55× smaller, because air is ~830× less dense.

cards.title: As temperature rises, what happens to the viscosity of a liquid, and of a gas?
cards.body:
Liquid: decreases. Gas: increases.
Liquid viscosity comes mainly from cohesive forces between molecules, which weaken as the molecules move faster. Gas viscosity comes from molecular collisions carrying momentum between layers, which intensify with temperature.
That's why motor oil thins out when hot.

cards.title: What is the gauge pressure at the bottom of a 10 m deep open tank of fresh water?
cards.body:
≈ 98.1 kPa (gauge).
P = P_atm + ρgh, so P_gauge = ρgh = 1000·9.81·10 = 98,100 Pa. Absolute: ≈ 101.3 + 98.1 = 199.4 kPa at sea level.
P_abs = P_atm + P_gauge; below atmospheric, P_abs = P_atm − P_vac. Pressure depends only on depth, not on the container's shape.

cards.title: A wooden block of density 600 kg/m³ floats in fresh water. What fraction of its volume is submerged?
cards.body:
0.6 (60%).
Archimedes: buoyant force = weight of the displaced fluid, F_B = ρ_fluid·g·V_sub, acting up through the centroid of the displaced volume. Floating: F_B = W, so ρ_w·V_sub = ρ_b·V, giving V_sub/V = ρ_b/ρ_w.
Trap: F_B uses the FLUID's density and the submerged volume, not the body's.

cards.title: A vertical rectangular gate 3 m tall has its top edge at the water's free surface. At what depth does the resultant hydrostatic force act?
cards.body:
2 m deep (2/3 of the height), below the centroid at 1.5 m.
Magnitude uses the centroid depth: F_R = ρg·h_C·A. Location (gauge pressure): y_P = y_C + I_xx,C/(y_C·A) = 1.5 + (b·3³/12)/(1.5·3b) = 2 m.
On any non-horizontal plane surface the center of pressure lies below the centroid, approaching it as the surface goes deeper.

cards.title: Water flows at 2 m/s in a 10 cm diameter pipe that narrows to 5 cm diameter. What is the velocity in the narrow section?
cards.body:
8 m/s.
Incompressible continuity: Q = A₁V₁ = A₂V₂, so V₂ = V₁(D₁/D₂)² = 2·(10/5)² = 8 m/s.
Trap: halving the diameter quarters the area, so the velocity rises 4×, not 2×. For compressible flow, conserve the mass flow rate ṁ = ρAV instead.

cards.title: What four assumptions must hold to use the Bernoulli equation P/ρ + V²/2 + gz = constant?
cards.body:
1) Steady flow. 2) Incompressible flow. 3) Negligible friction (viscous effects). 4) Applied along a streamline.
Also: no pump, turbine or heat transfer between the two points.
It fails in boundary layers, in long pipes with friction and across a pump or fan; use the energy equation with head loss h_L instead.

cards.title: A Pitot-static tube in air (ρ = 1.2 kg/m³) reads stagnation minus static pressure = 240 Pa. What is the air speed?
cards.body:
20 m/s.
Bernoulli from the free stream to the stagnation point (V = 0): P₀ = P + ½ρV², so V = √(2(P₀ − P)/ρ) = √(2·240/1.2) = √400 = 20 m/s.
Trap: use the density of the flowing fluid (air), not that of the manometer liquid.

cards.title: Water (ν = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s) flows at 0.1 m/s in a 2 cm diameter pipe. What is the Reynolds number?
cards.body:
2000, so laminar.
Re = VD/ν = ρVD/μ = (0.1)(0.02)/(10⁻⁶) = 2000: the ratio of inertial to viscous forces.
Circular pipes (Çengel): laminar for Re ≲ 2300, transitional ≈ 2300–4000, turbulent for Re ≳ 4000. These are approximate; transition depends on disturbances, wall roughness and vibration.

cards.title: Darcy friction factor for fully developed laminar flow in a circular pipe?
cards.body:
f = 64/Re.
In laminar flow it doesn't depend on wall roughness. Trap: the Fanning friction factor is 1/4 of Darcy's (16/Re), so check which one a chart or formula uses.
Turbulent: f depends on Re and relative roughness ε/D (Colebrook equation or Moody chart).

cards.title: Darcy–Weisbach equation: head loss h_L in a pipe of length L, diameter D, mean velocity V and friction factor f?
cards.body:
h_L = f(L/D)(V²/2g), in meters of fluid; as a pressure drop, ΔP_L = ρg·h_L = f(L/D)(ρV²/2).
Valid for laminar and turbulent flow. Laminar (f = 64/Re): h_L ∝ V. Fully rough turbulent (f constant): h_L ∝ V².
At a fixed flow rate in fully rough flow, h_L ∝ 1/D⁵: a slightly bigger pipe cuts losses a lot.

cards.title: What is the hydraulic diameter of a noncircular duct, and what does it reduce to for a circular pipe and for a square duct of side a?
cards.body:
D_h = 4A_c/p, where A_c is the flow area and p the wetted perimeter.
Circle: 4(πD²/4)/(πD) = D. Square: 4a²/(4a) = a.
Use D_h in place of D in Re and the Darcy–Weisbach equation. Laminar flow in noncircular ducts has its own f·Re value (≈ 57 for a square duct instead of 64).

cards.title: Drag force F_D = ½ρV²·C_D·A. If the speed doubles with C_D unchanged, by what factor does the drag force change?
cards.body:
4× (it quadruples).
F_D ∝ V², and the power needed to overcome drag, F_D·V, rises 8×.
A is the frontal area for blunt bodies (cars, spheres) but the planform area for wings and plates parallel to the flow. C_D itself varies with Re, so the V² scaling assumes C_D stays roughly constant.

packs.title: Digital Logic
packs.description: Hex and two's complement, overflow, De Morgan, NAND universality, parity, minterms and K-maps, adders, muxes, latches, flip-flops, timing, FSMs, counters.

cards.title: Convert the binary number 11010110 to hexadecimal.
cards.body:
D6 (= 214 in decimal).
Group the bits in fours starting from the binary point: 1101 0110 → D, 6. Pad the leftmost group with leading zeros if needed.
Check: 13·16 + 6 = 214 = 128 + 64 + 16 + 4 + 2.

cards.title: What is −6 in 8-bit two's complement?
cards.body:
1111 1010.
Negate by inverting every bit and adding 1: +6 = 0000 0110 → 1111 1001 → 1111 1010.
Shortcut: copy the bits from the right up to and including the first 1, then invert the rest. Check: −128 + 122 = −6.

cards.title: What range of integers can an 8-bit two's complement number represent?
cards.body:
−128 to +127.
n bits: −2ⁿ⁻¹ to 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1. There's one more negative value because zero uses a 'positive' pattern; −128 = 1000 0000 has no positive partner (negating it gives itself).
Unsigned 8-bit: 0 to 255. Sign-magnitude and 1's complement: −127 to +127 (they have two zeros).

cards.title: When adding two n-bit two's complement numbers, how do you detect overflow?
cards.body:
Overflow occurs when both operands have the same sign but the sum's sign bit differs. Hardware test: V = C_n ⊕ C_(n−1), i.e., the carry out of the MSB differs from the carry into it.
Adding numbers of opposite signs can never overflow.
Example, 4 bits: 0111 + 0001 = 1000, i.e., 7 + 1 → −8. The final carry-out alone does NOT indicate signed overflow.

cards.title: By De Morgan's theorem, the complement of a product, (AB)′, equals what?
cards.body:
A′ + B′.
Break the bar and change the operator: (AB)′ = A′ + B′ and (A + B)′ = A′B′. Works for any number of variables.
So a NAND gate is equivalent to an OR gate with inverted (bubbled) inputs, and a NOR gate to an AND gate with bubbled inputs.

cards.title: What is the minimum number of 2-input NAND gates needed to build a 2-input OR gate?
cards.body:
3.
A + B = (A′B′)′: two NANDs with tied inputs make A′ and B′, and a third NAND combines them.
NOT takes 1 NAND and AND takes 2, so NAND alone can build any Boolean function: it's a universal gate. NOR is universal too (by duality).

cards.title: What even-parity bit should be appended to the 7-bit data word 1011001?
cards.body:
0.
Even parity makes the total number of 1s even. The data already has four 1s, so P = 1⊕0⊕1⊕1⊕0⊕0⊕1 = 0.
A multi-input XOR outputs 1 when an odd number of its inputs are 1, which is why XOR trees generate and check parity. One parity bit detects any single-bit error, but not a double one.

cards.title: Simplify F(A, B, C) = Σm(1, 3, 5, 7) to a minimal sum of products.
cards.body:
F = C.
Minterms 1, 3, 5, 7 (001, 011, 101, 111) are exactly the rows where C = 1; A and B take every value, so they drop out.
Minterm mᵢ is a product term equal to 1 only in row i; maxterm Mᵢ is a sum term equal to 0 only in row i, and Mᵢ = mᵢ′. Same function in POS form: F = ΠM(0, 2, 4, 6).

cards.title: What are the rules for grouping 1s on a Karnaugh map to get a minimal sum of products?
cards.body:
Groups must be rectangles of 1, 2, 4, 8… cells (powers of 2). Adjacency wraps around the map's edges (Gray-code order 00, 01, 11, 10).
Make each group as large as possible and use as few groups as possible; groups may overlap; every 1 must be covered.
Don't-cares (X) may be included when they enlarge a group. A group of 2ᵏ cells eliminates k variables.

cards.title: Full adder with inputs A, B and C_in: what are the Boolean expressions for the sum S and the carry C_out?
cards.body:
S = A ⊕ B ⊕ C_in; C_out = AB + C_in(A ⊕ B), equivalent to the majority function AB + AC_in + BC_in.
It can be built from two half adders (each: S = A ⊕ B, C = AB) plus an OR gate on their carries.
Chaining n full adders makes an n-bit ripple-carry adder.

cards.title: How many select lines does a 16-to-1 multiplexer need?
cards.body:
4, since 2⁴ = 16: n select lines choose one of 2ⁿ data inputs.
A 2ⁿ-to-1 mux can implement any n-variable function by wiring the truth-table outputs to its data inputs.
Compare a decoder: n inputs, 2ⁿ outputs, each output one minterm, so a decoder plus an OR gate also implements any function.

cards.title: In an SR latch built from NOR gates, which input combination is not allowed, and why?
cards.body:
S = R = 1.
It forces both Q and Q′ to 0, so they're no longer complements; if S and R then return to 0 together, the next state is unpredictable (a race).
NAND (S′R′) latch: the forbidden input is S′ = R′ = 0. The JK flip-flop removes the problem: J = K = 1 toggles.

cards.title: Characteristic equation of a JK flip-flop: Q(t+1) = ?
cards.body:
Q(t+1) = JQ′ + K′Q.
JK = 00 hold, 10 set, 01 reset, 11 toggle.
Compare D: Q(t+1) = D (it just stores the input at the clock edge), and T: Q(t+1) = T ⊕ Q.

cards.title: Flip-flop timing: what are setup time and hold time?
cards.body:
Setup time: how long the input must be stable BEFORE the active clock edge. Hold time: how long it must stay stable AFTER the edge.
Violating either can make the flip-flop metastable.
Setup limits clock speed: T_clk ≥ t_clk-to-Q + t_logic,max + t_setup. Hold is checked on the shortest path: t_clk-to-Q + t_logic,min ≥ t_hold.

cards.title: In which type of finite-state machine do the outputs depend only on the present state, not on the current inputs?
cards.body:
Moore machine.
Mealy: outputs depend on the present state AND the inputs, so they can react within the same clock cycle and often need fewer states, but they can glitch when inputs change.
In a Moore state diagram the outputs are written inside the states; in a Mealy diagram, on the transitions (input/output).

cards.title: Minimum number of flip-flops needed for a mod-10 (decade) counter?
cards.body:
4.
n flip-flops have 2ⁿ states: 2³ = 8 < 10 ≤ 16 = 2⁴, so n = ⌈log₂ 10⌉ = 4.
A BCD counter counts 0000 to 1001 and returns to 0000 on the next clock; 6 of its 16 states (1010–1111) are unused. A mod-N counter divides the clock frequency by N.
